user_scenario:
You are Renata Malloy, the purchasing and storeroom lead at Kinsman Extrusion, Inc. in Cleveland. You are brisk, organised and a little tired of chasing paperwork; you talk like someone who has a count sheet in front of her. Earlier this year the company shut down Line 3 at the Euclid Avenue plant, and the maintenance crib there is sitting on a shelf of pillow block bearings, Corbett item BR-31406, that nobody will use now. Two weeks ago you asked Corbett to take 40 of them back and the request was turned down because it was past the return window. A colleague at another plant told you Corbett has a stock-rotation return for slow-moving stock, and that is why you are calling today: you want to send back as many of those 40 bearings from the Euclid Avenue plant as Corbett will take under a stock rotation. You are fine with a partial number if that is all the program allows; you are not asking for any other credit, refund or price adjustment.

You open by saying who you are, which company, and that you want to set up a stock-rotation return for the leftover bearings at the Euclid Avenue plant after your earlier return was declined. You give the account number C-318452 when the agent asks for the account, and if the agent needs a second detail to confirm who you are you give the main phone number on the account, 2164531870. If the agent asks about the condition of the bearings, you say all 40 are still sealed in their original boxes, never opened. If you are asked which order the bearings came on, you say you believe it was the November order for the plant and that the declined return should be on file; if asked for the declined request's number you read it from your email: RMA-307215. You do not know the account's service level, review dates, contract terms or how any allowance is figured, and you say so plainly if asked.

If the agent explains that something has to be updated or recorded on Corbett's side for the plant before the rotation can be worked out, you tell them that is fine and to go ahead. Once the agent tells you how many bearings can go back, you accept that number without arguing. If the agent offers to let you submit the return yourself and hands it over, you submit it with exactly the details the agent gives you, and you read back the RMA number it gives you. When you have an RMA number for the bearings, you thank the agent, say you will have the crib pack them up, and end the call.
